ranking.name: Uncertainty-adaptive caution margin for wave smoothing from roadside radar (line #3, re-scored)
ranking.plain_explanation: A wave-smoothing car drives more gently than normal cruise control (ACC). It uses a forecast of the traffic waves ahead, built from roadside radar (RDS). The forecast can be wrong, so the car keeps a caution margin: when it is unsure, it behaves more like ACC. A self-calibrating margin would grow when recent forecasts were bad and shrink when they were good. This only pays if forecast quality changes a lot from one wave to the next, and if simple traffic state (the congestion regime) cannot predict that change. Nobody has measured this yet.
ranking.gates: G1 4: not shown on real data. In the toy, the caution level clearly changes behaviour, but the forecast errors there are synthetic. G2 3.5: toy headroom of +2.5 to +6.8 points of EV energy over one fixed caution level, but only under an ASSUMED 8x spread in forecast-error size (exploratory, spent data, unreviewed). The best fixed caution gives only 4.0 % on TGSIM at a 60 m gap cap, which is below the 5 % kill line. A regime-lookup rival was not tested. Published I-24 results suggest the forecast itself is worth only a few points. G3 3: the field is dense. CIRCLES/Vanderbilt own the data and the 100-CAV test, and Toyota holds US 12,371,020 on stop-and-go mitigation. No paper found combines RDS forecast intervals with a conformal or chance-constrained caution on I-24 replay, but the search had a budget and was not exhaustive. G4 5: WaveX is CC BY 4.0 and unread, but has only 33 lane-day blocks at one site and is the last unread dataset. No throw-away data with both RDS and ground truth exists locally. G5 6: best title fit among the survivors. The build (forecaster, conformal layer, chance-constrained MPC, replay harness) is heavy for a solo part-time author before ITSC on 1 Mar 2027.
ranking.main_risk: The adaptive margin may reduce to a regime lookup table: if forecast-error size mostly follows the congestion state, a fixed table matches it, as happened with C4 and line #1. On top of that, the WaveX/CIRCLES group can publish the natural next step first. Replay cannot show a wave dissolving. Also, energy as the headline metric needs the supervisor's agreement under the claim bar under review (the project's default primary metric is delay including queues).
ranking.first_step: THE ONE RECOMMENDED KILL TEST (it tests the candidate, it is not a decision to build). (a) Author decides two things: whether I-24 MOTION INCEPTION v1.0.0 (free account; access delay, terms and dates [VERIFY], including no date overlap with WaveX) may be spent as throw-away screen data so that WaveX stays unread; and whether smoother energy is an acceptable outcome metric. (b) Claude commits the kill rules before any data: KILL if adaptive caution minus regime-lookup caution is under 2 points of EV energy at a 60 m gap cap, or if the best fixed caution is under 5 %. Then Claude builds virtual 30-s stations at 0.3-0.5 mi spacing, fits a point forecaster, measures how much forecast-error size varies across episodes and how much a speed-regime lookup explains, and re-runs smooth_fixed_vs_adaptive.py with the measured errors. (c) About 1 day of build and under 1 h of CPU.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating ramp queue-override (spill-back) margin
ranking.plain_explanation: Cars wait in a queue at a metered on-ramp. If the queue gets too long, it blocks the city street, so the meter starts releasing cars faster: this is called queue override. Override starts a safety margin before the ramp is full; MnDOT's open-source IRIS software keeps the queue at most 75 % full. A self-calibrating version would set this margin from how wrong the queue estimate has been recently. By a rough calculation, though, the margin only moves the override start by seconds, so the gain for freeway traffic is probably very small.
ranking.gates: G1 5: override is often active at one Caltrans site, but the margin WIDTH only shifts the timing of the decision. G2 2: a conservation bound (reasoning, with assumed numbers) gives about 0.1-0.5 % of bottleneck flow at best. Caveat: the bound ignores peaks where a narrower margin would avoid an override entirely, and the share of such near-threshold peaks is unmeasured. G3 5: academically sparse, but the anchor-corrected estimator and a fixed 25 % margin are already deployed in IRIS and published (Lee, Jiang, Chung 2013), so only the bound width is new. G4 5: Mayfly needs no account, but there is no ground-truth queue, the labels are censored and come from IRIS's own closed loop, and no data licence was found. G5 5: an algorithm, so V78 is met, but it is roadside infrastructure, and any delay claim needs a SUMO ramp-plus-arterial plant.
ranking.main_risk: Only a coverage claim (spill-back miss rate at or below alpha with a narrower margin) survives. That is a proxy-type headline, close to line #1's VALID-ONLY result, and it is incremental over deployed IRIS logic.
ranking.first_step: (b) Claude, 1-2 h, no traffic data opened: compute an analytic headroom bound. Inputs: public per-meter storage from the metro_config metadata, IRIS's 25 % margin and 140 veh/mile, literature ranges for excess arrivals, and Kan's 10 % discharge drop. Include the near-threshold-peak case. KILL if the upper bound is under 1 % of peak corridor delay (the rule is committed before computing). Only if it passes: (a) the author decides whether a coverage-only claim counts under the claim bar now under review.

ranking.name: Phase-aware self-calibrated critical-gap margin for an automated vehicle's permissive left turn
ranking.plain_explanation: An automated car turning left on a green light without an arrow must wait for a big enough gap in oncoming traffic. The smallest gap it accepts is the margin. A self-calibrating version would adjust this gap from how well the car has recently predicted when oncoming cars arrive, separately for each approach and signal phase. That could cut waiting time while keeping conflicts rare. But a fixed table per phase, which open-source Autoware already ships, will probably do just as well.
ranking.gates: G1 5: not measured on real data. A synthetic Poisson model only (not data) says a 0.5 s shift flips 4-12 % of decisions. G2 2: not measured, low prior. A phase-conditional fixed table or 'calibrate briefly, then freeze' is the expected winner, as in line #1 and screen #2. G3 3.5: on arXiv the exact combination returns 0 hits, but the method family is crowded (Conformal Decision Theory, ACI motion planning, CoCoNav). Wang & Zhang 2026 already adapt permissive-left safety buffers with PID toward a target risk. Autoware ships phase-conditioned margins, and patents exist (GM US 10,198,002; Waymo US 12,252,158; incomplete). G4 4: the NGSIM Lankershim/Peachtree rows are on disk and unread, but they hold a few hundred decisions at most. SinD needs an application and its licence is unclear, and Waymo Open Motion has no per-approach continuity. G5 7: strong title fit, but the evaluation is semi-synthetic replay and the core risks drifting toward a measurement study.
ranking.main_risk: No headroom over a phase table (another VALID-ONLY result), plus near-neighbour prior work on adaptive left-turn buffers. Non-reactive replay limits any guarantee to the replay model.
ranking.first_step: (a) Author designates the NGSIM Lankershim/Peachtree rows as throw-away. (b) Claude first checks, in about 1 h and without parsing trajectories, whether the NGSIM signal-timing files give per-second phase states. If they do not, the phase-aware part cannot be screened on this data, so stop. Kill rules are fixed before any rows are parsed: G1 KILL if under 2 % of decisions flip under a +/-0.5 s change; G2 STOP if a hindsight time-varying margin beats a hindsight phase table by under 2 decision points.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating automatic incident detection (AID) threshold with false-alarm-rate control
ranking.plain_explanation: Traffic centres run software that raises an alarm when loop-detector data suggest a crash or incident. The alarm threshold is the margin: set it too low and there are many false alarms, too high and real incidents are missed. A self-calibrating version would keep false alarms at a fixed budget per station while detecting incidents as fast as possible. It is not a driving algorithm, and IBM already patented statistically estimated, time-varying per-location thresholds.
ranking.gates: G1 7: a threshold decides every alarm, but the signal is weak (TraffiDent's best 3-class accuracy is 41.6 %). G2 2: arithmetic, not data. At 1 false alarm per station-week, each time-of-day stratum needs about 24 weeks of clean data, so 'online' becomes 'calibrate, then freeze'. G3 3: IBM US 9,207,105 covers the frozen rival, and quickest-change detection for AID goes back to at least 2003. G4 6: XTraffic is public (about 10 GB, CC BY-NC 4.0, unread), but has only 5-min data for one year and first-report incident times. G5 3: an alarm for operators, not a driving algorithm.
ranking.main_risk: Killed. It could be revived only if the supervisor accepts a detection algorithm under the title AND a label-free screen shows null drift within weeks.
ranking.first_step: None (drop). Revival test only if the supervisor accepts detection work: a label-free null-drift screen on one XTraffic district, as described in the refutation.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating freeway queue-warning (end-of-queue) activation threshold
ranking.plain_explanation: Roadside signs warn drivers about a stopped queue ahead. The sign switches on when a risk score from detectors passes a threshold, and that threshold is the margin. A self-calibrating version would hold the missed-warning rate at a target while showing as few needless warnings as possible. The evidence says thresholds work after a one-time calibration at each new site, which is the frozen rival.
ranking.gates: G1 4: weak score skill in NGSIM, and MnDOT policy overrides and up to 1 min of sign latency mute the threshold. G2 2: at the new MnDOT site the thresholds were already recalibrated and detection stayed poor, because the model fitted to the original site did not transfer. TTI found a yearly refresh best, and Basso et al. 2026 found cumulative retraining beats adaptive drift detection (abstract only). The scouts' NGSIM headroom is an artefact. G3 5: few arXiv papers, but crowded in journals, and INRIX, HERE and TomTom sell end-of-queue alerts. G4 3: labels from Mayfly would be circular (no speeds, stations 660-890 m apart). G5 3: a roadside alarm judged as a classification result, which is a V78 risk.
ranking.main_risk: Killed. It could be revived only if the author rules that it counts under V78, a non-circular label source exists, and within-site drift is shown above an odd/even noise floor.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating rear-gap acceptance margin for automated lane change / ramp merge (UN R79-style)
ranking.plain_explanation: Before an automated car changes lane, it checks that the car coming from behind is far enough away. The rule (UN R79, as quoted by JRC) mixes a fixed 1 s time gap with constants for how hard the rear driver brakes. A self-calibrating version would learn those braking constants from data. In real data, only the fixed 1 s part decides anything, and being stricter does not reduce rear braking.
ranking.gates: G1 5: the margin binds in about 1/3 of NGSIM lane changes, but 95 % of that binding comes from the fixed t_G*v term. The learnable constants (a, t_B) change under 2 % of decisions. G2 1.5: in 4 of 6 site x speed cells, the strictest margin has equal or higher attributable rear braking than accepting every human gap, and a frozen rule ties on US-101. G3 3.5: Honda, Mobileye, DENSO, Toyota and Aptiv patents (front pages read; incomplete), plus conformal merging on real data (Bang et al. 2024). G4 5: refused gaps are never observed. MiTra is one day, and exiD is gated. G5 3.5: needs a closed-loop rear-driver model, so the result would follow that model. All numbers are exploratory, spent data, unreviewed.
ranking.main_risk: Killed. Free-flow, large-speed-difference traffic is untested, but the censoring problem stays.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating bus-priority arrival window (ETA margin in transit signal priority)
ranking.plain_explanation: A bus asks the traffic light for priority, and the controller keeps a time window around the bus's expected arrival. The window width is the margin. On Hamburg data, a fixed per-signal window works as well as any time-varying or online one.
ranking.gates: Scout scores, not separately refuted: G1 8 (the margin changes the decision for 50.8 % of trips). G2 1, MEASURED (exploratory, spent Hamburg 2023, unreviewed): the best time-varying hindsight window is only 1.9 % narrower than the hindsight constant, and the transferred fixed window is already 1.4 % narrower. G3 5. G4 6. G5 5.
ranking.main_risk: Killed by a measured G2. Any remaining gain lies in point ETA prediction, not in the margin.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating ALINEA set-point margin
ranking.plain_explanation: A ramp meter (ALINEA) tries to hold the freeway just below its critical occupancy, and the distance below it is the margin. Learning that set-point online is already published with a stability proof. Gains over fixed tuning were small and patternless.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 7; G2 3 (Hadi et al. 2015 found limited gains with no clear pattern); G3 2 (Tajdari & Roncoli, IEEE T-ITS 2023, online set-point estimation; AD-ALINEA from 2004); G4 5; G5 5.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating VSL / speed-harmonisation activation threshold
ranking.plain_explanation: Variable speed limits switch on when traffic gets close to breakdown, and how close is the margin. Simulation studies found only small gains, and real effects depend on driver compliance. It also repeats a path this PhD already dropped (V15).
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 6; G2 2; G3 4; G4 4 (no multi-day spent loop data available); G5 4.
ranking.main_risk: Killed on G2; the counterfactual depends entirely on simulation.

ranking.name: Leader-braking margin for a heavy-vehicle ego with weaker braking
ranking.plain_explanation: This is line #1's car-following margin, applied to a truck that brakes less hard. It almost never exceeds a normal truck following gap. The same frozen rival is expected to win.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 3.5 (0 % of windows above 2 m + 1.5 s*v for own braking of 3 m/s2 or more; exploratory, spent TGSIM); G2 2; G3 4; G4 4; G5 4.5.

ranking.name: Self-tuning passage time (gap-out threshold) for actuated signals
ranking.plain_explanation: An actuated traffic light ends a green phase when no car has arrived for a set time, and that time is the margin. In Hamburg data, it changes mostly with time of day, which a fixed table already captures. It is also signal-control work that overlaps the secondary v6 line.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 6; G2 2 (the 85th-percentile headway moves a median 1.0 s from week to week but 5 s across time bands; exploratory, spent Hamburg); G3 6; G4 4; G5 3.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating yellow / all-red clearance
ranking.plain_explanation: The yellow and all-red times protect drivers caught near the stop line. Drivers adapt to the yellow length, so observational data cannot show the gain, and the values are regulated. Safety changes would also need field tests.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 3; G2 2; G3 3; G4 3; G5 2.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating pedestrian clearance time
ranking.plain_explanation: The pedestrian crossing time assumes a walking speed, and that assumption is the margin. The useful adaptive version detects individual slow walkers, which is detection rather than calibration. No public data with pedestrian trajectories and signal states at scale was found.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 3; G2 2; G3 4; G4 2; G5 2 (close to a measurement study, V78).

ranking.name: Driver-adaptive forward-collision-warning timing
ranking.plain_explanation: A collision warning that fires too early annoys drivers, and one that fires too late misses danger. Adapting its timing to each driver needs per-driver response data, which is restricted. It is a warning, not a driving algorithm.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 6; G2 2; G3 2.5 (OpenAlex 48, three AAP papers on personalised FCW); G4 1.5; G5 2.5.

ranking.plain_explanation: Connected cars following closely need a bigger gap when messages arrive late or get lost. No public data pairs real message delay traces with trajectories, so any evidence would come from simulation only. The area is also crowded.

ranking.name: Curve / friction speed margin
ranking.plain_explanation: In a curve, a car should use only part of the available tyre grip, and that part is the margin. No public, unread data pairs measured friction with curve trajectories. It would be simulation-only.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 2; G2 2; G3 3.5; G4 1; G5 3.

ranking.name: Self-calibrating speed band for predictive eco-cruise of heavy trucks
ranking.plain_explanation: Truck eco-cruise lets the speed vary inside a band on hills to save fuel, and the band is the margin. OEMs hold many patents on this, and online tuning of eco-cruise MPC is already published. There is no outcome data on energy, only an assumed powertrain model.
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 7; G2 3; G3 1 (Daimler US6990401B2 and others; incomplete); G4 3; G5 5.

ranking.name: Weather / low-friction safe-speed margin
ranking.plain_explanation: In bad weather, the advised safe speed keeps a margin below what the road allows. The key datasets are restricted, and crashes are too rare to measure. A quantile-margin version is already published (arXiv 2602.05053).
ranking.gates: Scout scores: G1 4; G2 2; G3 3; G4 1 (Wyoming CV Pilot data restricted); G5 4.

ranked.honest_bottom_line:
No candidate passes all five gates convincingly, so none is recommended for a build. After the refutations, the best minimum gate score is 3 (open-C, wave-smoothing caution margin). The best G2 (headroom) score among all 18 candidates is only 3.5, and that 3.5 comes from a toy model with an assumed error spread, not from data.

Every margin domain checked shows the same pattern: line #1, screen #2, the bus-priority window (measured), queue warning, incident detection, the lane-change gap and the left turn. In each one, the strongest evidence points to a fixed per-site or per-regime table, or to 'calibrate once, then freeze', matching online self-calibration.

Reasoning (not a measured fact): a margin is a quantile of an error distribution. If that distribution is stable within a site, or is explained by a few observable regimes, then a threshold fitted once already gives the same guarantee. Online self-calibration only pays when there is drift within a site that the regime does not explain, and no scout found evidence of such drift in any domain. So the problem may be the 'self-calibrated margin' theme itself, not the particular candidates. That is worth bringing to the supervisor, together with the claim-bar question.

If the theme is kept, I recommend exactly one kill test, on open-C. The test measures how much real RDS-forecast error varies from episode to episode, and how much a speed-regime lookup already explains. It needs an author decision to spend I-24 MOTION INCEPTION as throw-away data (access, terms and dates [VERIFY]). It costs about 1 day of build and under 1 h of CPU. KILL if adaptive caution minus regime-lookup caution is under 2 points of energy, or if the best fixed caution is under 5 %.

Even if open-C passes, its scoop risk from the CIRCLES/Vanderbilt group and its heavy build remain. A pass would justify a protocol, not a claim.

fw-F1 and int-C3 stay possible only as weak fallbacks. Each has a cheaper desk or metadata check (an analytic bound for fw-F1; a signal-timing format check for int-C3), but both are expected to end VALID-ONLY. All exploratory numbers are on spent data and unreviewed, and all gate scores are subjective scores from several agents, not calibrated against each other.
completeness_gaps: Patents are incomplete for every candidate: Google Patents was deliberately not queried from this machine. Patent signals come from a few WebSearches and USPTO or EPO front pages, and Justia returned 403. Claims and legal status were mostly unread, for example IBM US 9,207,105 (in force or lapsed is unknown), Waymo US 12,252,158 beyond claims 1, 8 and 9, and US 11,614,739.

G1 is not measured on real data for any survivor. open-C's binding comes from synthetic forecast errors. int-C3 has only a synthetic Poisson model, with no spent intersection trajectories. For fw-F1, the share of MnDOT peaks with queue occupancy above 25 % is unmeasured.

G2 is not measured on real data for any survivor. open-C rests on an ASSUMED 8x spread in forecast error, and no regime-lookup rival was tested. fw-F1 rests on a conservation bound with assumed arrival rates, which ignores peaks where a narrower margin would avoid an override entirely. int-C3 rests on a low prior only.

arXiv is a poor proxy for fields that publish in TRR, TR-C and agency reports (ramp metering, queue warning, AID). Counts swing about 4x with phrasing. Several queries were polluted ('critical gap', conform* matching conformal field theory). The open-C check hit HTTP 429 and could not reproduce the scout's exact query. Two earlier counts were wrong and were corrected ('collision warning' 3 -> 38; 'lane change + conformal' 219 -> 1).

Literature checks ran on a per-agent WebSearch budget and are not systematic reviews. Statements that no source was found for a given combination are search results, not proof of absence. No first/novel claims can be made.

Unverified items [VERIFY]: I-24 MOTION INCEPTION access, terms, approval delay and dates (needed for the recommended kill test; i24motion.org gave a certificate error). Whether NGSIM Lankershim/Peachtree signal timings give per-second phase states. SinD licence and access delay. MnDOT/Mayfly data licence. Whether meter phase and rate logs are on Mayfly. Which IRIS version MnDOT ran in a given year. The UN R79 regulation text (constants quoted via JRC/Cellina). The SinD 2.0 per-site gap-mining claim. The ICLR AdaptNC link (the cited arXiv 2504.00447 is a different paper, Egocentric Conformal Prediction).

Papers read as abstract or snippet only: Wang & Zhang 2026 (permissive-left PID buffers; abstract read from the PDF), Basso et al. 2026, Robbennolt & Hourdos 2023 TRR (full text), the TTI 0-4770-1 full report, Bang/Dave/Malikopoulos 2024, Lee/Jiang/Chung 2013, Spiliopoulou et al. 2010, Li/Nishi et al. (SSRN abstract not available), and Carpio 2025 (affiliation).

The refuters' own scripts are exploratory and have not been independently reviewed: smooth_attack.py, smooth_fixed_vs_adaptive.py, qw_ngsim_check.py, lc_adv.py, lc_adv_stats*.py, far_math.py and g1_model.py.
The 12 synthesis-dropped candidates (C1, F3, F4, C-H, C2, C4, C5, C-F, C-V, C-C, D, E) carry scout scores only; no separate refutation round was run on them. Only C1 has a measured G2 kill.

top.summary: Ranked 1 of 6. How the list was built: candidates are ordered by their minimum gate score. Ties are broken leximin: the second-lowest gate first, then the third-lowest. The margin is the queue-override trigger: a preset occupancy threshold on the queue detector(s) upstream of ramp storage, plus MnDOT's wait-time limits (4 min per vehicle on local ramps, 2 min on freeway-to-freeway ramps). Operations engineers set it per ramp by hand, and MnDOT's exact trigger values are not public [VERIFY]. Proposed algorithm: a per-ramp online queue estimate (conservation from Queue/Passage/Green detector counts, with a Kalman update in the style of Lee, Jiang and Chung 2013 [VERIFY]), wrapped in an online-calibrated error bound (online quantile or adaptive conformal). The bound is refitted from anchor events: queue-detector occupancy saturating, or the ramp emptying. The override fires when the estimate exceeds storage minus the bound. The target is a spill-back miss rate of at most alpha with less override time than a fixed threshold. Strongest simple rival: a per-ramp fixed margin over a Kalman estimate, calibrated on the first 2 weeks and then frozen; a second rival is the Spiliopoulou-style queue controller with a fixed safety margin. Weakest gate: G2. Headroom is unknown and only plausible; the line #1 and Hamburg lessons favour the freeze rival. Converting margin width into delay needs a SUMO ramp-merge plant. The PhD prior for gains over fixed parameters is 1.5-6 % published and 0-5 % in the three v6 gates. Title fit is moderate, because this is infrastructure control rather than a vehicle algorithm.
evidence: G1, fact: Kan, Lu, Skabardonis, TRB 2019 paper 19-05057 (2 weeks of video at a San Jose metered merge): 'bottleneck discharge flow is reduced by 10% on the average when the queue override is activated'. https://path.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/paper_19-05057_final_impact_of_queue_override.pdf

G1, fact: Daines, Schultz, Macfarlane 2022 (Future Transportation): Kalman and heuristic queue estimates were 'generally within about eight vehicles' of the observed queues on I-15. https://doi.org/10.3390/futuretransp2040045 [VERIFY, seen via a search summary]. Reasoning (scout): against 10-30 vehicles of storage, that error is a large share of the margin.

G1, own archive, simulation only: in the day-pattern testbed T0 KILL, with 10-23 vehicles of ramp storage and a 240-s wait limit, the queue layer released held vehicles almost at once, so the queue limit dominated metering. claude/day-pattern-core:docs/lab/day_pattern/testbed_screen.md. top.summary: Ranked 6 of 6 (minimum 2.5; sorted scores 2.5,4.5,5.5,6,8). It is the only candidate at 2.5; every candidate below it has a minimum of 2 or less. The margin is the UN R79 critical distance to the approaching rear vehicle: S_crit = (v_app - v_ALC)*t_B + (v_app - v_ALC)^2/(2a) + v_ALC*t_G, with a = 3 m/s^2, t_B = 0.4 s, t_G = 1 s, as quoted by Cellina et al. (JRC); the regulation itself was not read [VERIFY]. Proposed algorithm: accept a gap only if an upper conformal or online-quantile bound on the rear vehicle's response (induced deceleration or post-merge minimum time gap) stays inside a budget. The bound is conditioned on speed bin, relative speed and ramp vs mainline; the step is batch-normalised; the decision is a closed-form rule. G1 passes strongly on spent NGSIM: R79 would refuse about a third of the gaps humans take. Weakest gate: G2, which likely FAILS on spent data. attacks.finding: The two core pieces of the 'self-calibrating' estimator are already deployed and published. MnDOT's own open-source ATMS, IRIS, runs a conservation queue estimate from queue, passage and green counts. It corrects that estimate online at exactly the proposed anchor events: queue-detector occupancy above 25% raises the estimate towards maximum storage, and an empty-queue test pulls demand back to passage. It also holds a FIXED margin: the queue storage limit keeps the queue at most 75% full, and the wait target is 75% of max wait. Lee, Jiang and Chung (2013) published the same pattern: a conservation Kalman filter, an occupancy update, and a 'singular-point correction' that resets the accumulated counting error. What is left to contribute is only the width of the error bound (an online quantile or conformal bound in place of 25%). That is a thin increment.

attacks.finding: Under a hard no-spill-back rule, conservation fixes the long-run ramp release at ramp demand. The margin only sets how much of the buffer is used. The archive's own T0 KILL points the same way: there, the WHOLE 10-23-vehicle storage could not move bottleneck inflow. A margin that is a fraction of that storage moves even less. On top of an IRIS-style anchor-corrected queue estimate, an online-calibrated bound could keep the rate at which the queue reaches the detector at or below alpha, at a width below IRIS's fixed 25% storage margin. candidates.name: F1. Self-calibrating ramp queue-override (spill-back) margin
candidates.margin: The queue-override trigger: today a preset occupancy threshold on the queue detector(s) upstream of ramp storage (described in eprints.soton.ac.uk/53259 and in Kan, Lu, Skabardonis 2019), plus MnDOT's wait-time limits: 'four minutes per vehicle on local ramps' and 'two minutes per vehicle on freeway-to-freeway ramps' (dot.state.mn.us/rampmeter). Agency operations engineers set it per ramp by hand. MnDOT's exact trigger values are not public in anything I found [VERIFY].
candidates.algorithm: A per-ramp online queue estimate: conservation from the Queue, Passage and Green detector counts, with a Kalman update in the style of Lee, Jiang and Chung 2013 [VERIFY]. Around it, an online-calibrated error bound (online quantile or adaptive conformal), refitted from recent 'anchor' events where the queue is known, such as queue-detector occupancy saturating (queue at the storage limit) or the ramp emptying. Override fires when the estimate exceeds storage minus the calibrated bound. Target: spill-back miss rate at most alpha, with less override time than a fixed threshold. Reasoning: each override is costly (about 10 % discharge loss in one field study), so a margin that tightens when the estimate is good and widens when counts drift is the self-calibration payoff.
candidates.G1_binds: Likely binds; not yet measured on public data. Facts: (1) Kan, Lu, Skabardonis (TRB 2019, paper 19-05057, 2 weeks of video at a San Jose metered merge): 'bottleneck discharge flow is reduced by 10% on the average when the queue override is activated'. (2) Daines, Schultz, Macfarlane 2022 (Future Transportation, doi 10.3390/futuretransp2040045; seen only through a search summary [VERIFY]): Kalman and heuristic queue estimates were 'generally within about eight vehicles' of observed queues on I-15. Reasoning: against 10-30 vehicles of storage, that error is a large share of the margin. (3) Own archive, simulation only: the day-pattern testbed T0 KILL found that with 10-23 vehicles of ramp storage and a 240-s wait limit, the queue layer released held vehicles almost at once (claude/day-pattern-core:docs/lab/day_pattern/testbed_screen.md). So the queue limit dominated metering there. Unknown: the share of MnDOT peak periods with override events.
candidates.G2_headroom: Unknown, plausible, not yet tested. Headroom exists only if the queue-estimate error changes within or across days (count drift, congestion level), so that a per-ramp fixed margin is too wide on some days or misses on others. The line #1 and Hamburg lessons say per-site fixed margins often transfer, and a 'calibrate on the first N days, then freeze' rival is the main threat. The throughput side (less override time means more metering authority) needs a counterfactual. Data alone give only the coverage and width of the margin. Converting width into delay needs a ramp-merge simulation, and in this PhD the prior for control gains over fixed parameters is 1.5-6 % published, 0-5 % in three v6 gates (CLAUDE.md).

candidates.name: C-M: Self-calibrating rear-gap acceptance margin for automated lane change / ramp merge (UN R79-style critical distance with constants learned from the rear driver's response)
candidates.margin: The R79 'Suppression of the Lane Change Procedure' critical distance to the approaching rear vehicle: S_crit = (v_app - v_ALC)*t_B + (v_app - v_ALC)^2/(2a) + v_ALC*t_G, with a = 3 m/s^2 (assumed maximum deceleration of the rear vehicle), t_B = 0.4 s, t_G = 1 s. The values are set by the regulator (UNECE R79, as quoted by Cellina et al., JRC, arXiv 2608.26669; I have not read the regulation text [VERIFY]). OEMs also use fixed thresholds on the deceleration the trailing vehicle would need (GM US 11046321, per search snippet [VERIFY]).
candidates.algorithm: Accept a gap only if an upper conformal / online-quantile bound on the rear vehicle's response stays inside a safety budget. Two possible targets: the rear driver's induced deceleration, or the post-merge minimum time gap. The bound is conditioned on context: speed bin, relative speed, ramp vs mainline. The step is batch-normalised, which repairs the line-#1 flaw. Equivalently, it learns (a, t_B, t_G) online per context, with a finite-sample miss-rate statement. The decision layer is a closed-form gap rule; no NN is needed.
candidates.G1_binds: PASSES (exploratory, spent data, unreviewed). On NGSIM I-80 + US-101 there are 3,725 usable human lane changes (lane stable 2 s before and after; lag vehicle from the 'Following' field). 34.2 % of them had a rear gap below the R79 S_crit at the lane switch: 31 % on I-80, 39 % on US-101. For ramp merges (566, lane 7 [VERIFY lane coding]) the share is 44.5 %. The share rises with speed: 5-27 % below 5 m/s, 50-54 % above 15 m/s. An R79-bound AV would therefore refuse about a third of the gaps humans take. Observed rear-vehicle 1-s deceleration after the lane change: median 0.95, p90 2.0, p95 2.5, p99 4.3 m/s^2. So R79's a = 3 m/s^2 sits near the 96th-97th percentile. NGSIM's speed and acceleration noise is well known; this is congested traffic only.
candidates.G2_headroom:
LIKELY FAILS against the best per-site fixed margin (exploratory, spent data, unreviewed). Rule family: accept iff gap >= dv+*0.4 + dv+^2/6 + v*theta.
(1) With outcomes not mechanically tied to the gap, the margin barely predicts risk. Outcome 'rear braking > 2 m/s^2 and > 0.5 m/s^2 above its own pre-change braking': 6.8 % when R79 is not violated vs 8.2 % when it is. Outcome 'gap shrinks from >= 0.8 s to < 0.5 s': 1.0 % vs 2.4 %. Base rates are 4.5-9 %. In most site × alpha cells, theta = -0.5 s (accept every human gap) already meets alpha = 0.05-0.10. Headroom over a single fixed theta is 0 in those cells. In the one exception (I-80, alpha 0.05) no theta reaches alpha. So the margin is not the lever on the outcome.
(2) Only the outcome 'rear min time gap < 0.5 s or decel > 3' (partly tautological with the gap) shows context headroom: I-80 hindsight per-speed-bin theta accepts 63.6 % vs 37.9 % for one theta at alpha 0.05. On US-101 the gain is about 0.
(3) Non-transfer exists, as in line #1: theta fitted on US-101 under-covers I-80 (9.7 % vs a 5 % target). That again points to a VALID-ONLY result, not a win.
Reasoning: against the R79 constants the headroom is large (about 34 % more gaps at similar observed risk), but G2 requires beating the best tuned fixed margin. A per-site 'fit once, freeze' rival would probably match the online rule.

candidates.algorithm: Score s_t comes from sparse stations: the 30-s speed drop between consecutive stations plus the occupancy trend. The alarm is on while s_t >= theta_t. theta_t is set by online conformal risk control (adaptive conformal inference with delayed labels), so the share of vehicles that needed a warning but got none stays <= alpha while alarm time is kept as low as possible. The labels ('this vehicle should have been warned') arrive minutes later from downstream data, using the Robbennolt & Hourdos 2023 hypothetical-trajectory method. Separate thresholds per context group: lane, and free-flow-to-queue versus congested. An optional driving layer: a CAV that receives the alarm starts to slow down early, and the same margin sets when it starts. No neural network is needed.
candidates.G1_binds: It binds by construction: theta decides every alarm, and the MnDOT transfer shows that the threshold choice moves detection and false alarms by tens of points. Binding in the useful sense, meaning better decisions than chance, is NOT shown yet. Exploratory, spent data, unreviewed: NGSIM I-80 and US-101, two virtual detectors 300 m apart, 30-s windows; script /tmp/claude-1000/-srv-shared-Workspace-phd-phd-speed-harmo-v5b1/59738c75-cfe8-434e-99ee-b78b7087de37/scratchpad/wf9/scripts/qwarn_ngsim.py, results qwarn_dv7.json and qwarn_dv10.json in the same folder. With 'needs warning' defined as a speed drop >= 7 m/s within 6 s (18-31 % of vehicles), the best Youden J was 0.13 and 0.12 for the two I-80 blocks and 0.01 for US-101. With >= 10 m/s (2.5-3.5 % of vehicles), J was 0.20 and 0.25 for I-80 and 0.00 for US-101. On short segments that are congested throughout, the detector score barely separates the vehicles. NGSIM has no free-flow-to-queue transitions, so this neither passes nor kills G1.
candidates.G2_headroom: Unknown and at risk. Exploratory result on the same spent data, unreviewed: a threshold tuned at one site loses up to 0.20 J at the other site. Within I-80, using the other block's threshold loses only 0.02-0.09 J, and this rests on few events (about 35-55 hard-braking vehicles per block, clustered in a handful of waves). This is the same pattern line #1 and screen #2 found: thresholds fail across sites, while a per-site frozen threshold stays close. MnDOT's own remedy (recalibrate at the new site, then run) IS the freeze rival. Reasoning: headroom could exist only if conditions change within a site, such as construction, season or detector drift. MnDOT notes that a 4-year reconstruction changed congestion at the second site. That is not evidence of headroom.

Separate groups by time of day and weather. Labels are incident logs.

candidates.name: C. Uncertainty-adaptive caution margin for wave smoothing from roadside radar on WaveX (line #3, re-scored; WaveX metadata only)
candidates.margin: The caution margin (a speed envelope or gap bound) that a smoothing vehicle keeps around its forecast of the waves ahead. Reasoning: in published smoothers this is a fixed design constant [VERIFY]. Line #3 would scale it with the forecast's uncertainty.
candidates.algorithm: Forecast the leader's speed 1-4 min ahead from RDS radar only (adaptive smoothing or EnKF, or samples from a diffusion reconstruction), then conformal intervals, then an MPC with chance limits on entering the slow region and on the maximum gap.
